snapshot.title: TNPSC Polity: FR, FD & DPSP
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ TNPSC Polity Hook: 17: Untouchability. 32: Remedies. 42nd: Duties. 44: Property out. 51A: Duties. 20/21: Safe.

quick_notes.title: Fundamental Rights (Art 12–35)
quick_notes.detail: Part III (Magna Carta of India). Art 14 (Equality), 17 (Untouchability), 19 (Freedoms), 21 (Life), 32 (Constitutional Remedies).
quick_notes.explanation: Fundamental Rights (FR) are a set of basic freedoms guaranteed to every person in India by the Constitution, found in Articles 12 to 35, which together form Part III of the Constitution. Part III is often called the Magna Carta of India because, just like the historic English Magna Carta protected rights against the king, Part III protects citizens against unfair government actions. Article 14 guarantees the right to equality, meaning the government must treat all people equally under the same law. Article 17 abolishes the practice of untouchability, which is the social discrimination against certain castes, and makes it a punishable offense. Article 19 gives citizens six specific freedoms, such as the freedom to speak, assemble peacefully, and move freely anywhere in India. Article 21 protects every person's right to life and personal liberty, meaning no one can be killed or imprisoned except by a fair legal procedure. Finally, Article 32 gives every person the right to directly approach the Supreme Court if any of these Fundamental Rights are violated, making it the most important right for enforcing all others.

quick_notes.title: DPSP (Art 36–51)
quick_notes.detail: Part IV. Non-justiciable. Dr. Ambedkar called them "Novel Features". Art 40 (Panchayats), 44 (UCC), 45 (Education).
quick_notes.explanation: The Directive Principles of State Policy, or DPSP, are a set of instructions in Part IV of the Indian Constitution, from Article 36 to Article 51. Unlike the Fundamental Rights (FR), which are enforceable by courts, the DPSP are non-justiciable, meaning a citizen cannot go to court to force the government to follow them. Dr. B. R. Ambedkar called these principles the "Novel Features" of the Constitution because they were a new and unique addition. Article 40 directs the state to organize village panchayats, which are local self-government bodies. Article 44 directs the state to work toward a Uniform Civil Code (UCC), which would be one set of personal laws for all citizens. Article 45 originally directed the state to provide free and compulsory education for all children until age fourteen, though this duty is now covered under the Fundamental Right to Education in Article 21A.

quick_notes.title: Fundamental Duties (Art 51A)
quick_notes.detail: Part IVA. Added by 42nd Amendment (1976) on Swaran Singh Committee recommendation. 11th duty added by 86th Amendment.
quick_notes.explanation: Fundamental Duties are a set of responsibilities for every Indian citizen, and they are listed in Article 51A of the Constitution. Article 51A is located in Part IVA of the Constitution, which is the section that contains these duties. The 42nd Amendment to the Constitution, made in 1976, added Part IVA and Article 51A, based on the recommendation of a committee led by Swaran Singh. Initially, there were ten duties, but the 86th Amendment to the Constitution, made in 2002, added an eleventh duty to the list.

quick_notes.title: Writs (Art 32 & 226)
quick_notes.detail: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo-Warranto. SC (Art 32) and HC (Art 226) power.
quick_notes.explanation: Writs are legal orders issued by courts to enforce Fundamental Rights (FR), which are the basic rights guaranteed to every citizen by the Constitution. The Supreme Court (SC) can issue writs under Article 32, and High Courts (HC) can issue them under Article 226. There are five types of writs: Habeas Corpus, which means "produce the body" and orders a person who is detained to be brought before a court to check if the detention is legal; Mandamus, which means "we command" and orders a public official to do a duty they are legally required to do; Prohibition, which stops a lower court from exceeding its authority; Certiorari, which means "to be informed" and allows a higher court to review and cancel a decision made by a lower court; and Quo-Warranto, which means "by what authority" and asks a person holding a public office to prove they have the legal right to hold that position. Under Article 32, the Supreme Court can issue these writs only for enforcing Fundamental Rights, while under Article 226, a High Court can issue them for enforcing Fundamental Rights or for any other legal purpose.

quick_notes.title: Suspension of Rights
quick_notes.detail: During Emergency (Art 352), all rights can be suspended EXCEPT Art 20 and 21.
quick_notes.explanation: During a National Emergency, which is declared under Article 352 of the Constitution when the security of India is threatened by war, external aggression, or armed rebellion, the government can temporarily stop or suspend most of the Fundamental Rights (FR) that are guaranteed to citizens. Fundamental Rights are the basic human rights, like freedom of speech or the right to equality, that are written in Part III of the Constitution. However, two very important rights can never be suspended, even during an Emergency: Article 20, which protects a person from being punished for a law that did not exist at the time of the crime and from being punished twice for the same offense, and Article 21, which guarantees that no person can be deprived of their life or personal liberty except according to a fair procedure established by law. This means that even in a crisis, the government cannot take away your protection against unfair criminal laws or your right to life and freedom.
